title: Poly- and heterofunctional compounds as metabolites and drugs

goals.text: To teach the student the structure, properties and significance as metabolites and drugs of compounds that contain identical (polyfunctional) or different (heterofunctional) functional groups — polyhydric alcohols and phenols, polyamines, dicarboxylic acids, amino alcohols and catecholamines, hydroxy-, amino- and keto acids, and heterofunctional derivatives of benzene.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the concept of poly- and heterofunctional compounds;
the properties and medical significance of glycerol, ethylene glycol, xylitol, sorbitol and mannitol;
polyhydric phenols and the quinone–hydroquinone redox system;
the significance of polyamines and dicarboxylic acids (oxalate, malonate, succinate, fumarate);
amino alcohols (ethanolamine, choline, acetylcholine) and catecholamines;
hydroxy and keto acids, and derivatives of salicylic and p-aminobenzoic acid.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify the functional groups of a compound and classify it;
explain the detection of polyhydric alcohols by the qualitative reaction with Cu(OH)~2~;
write interconversions of metabolites (lactate ⇄ pyruvate, succinate → fumarate);
link the chemical structure of drugs (aspirin, paracetamol, sulfonamides) with their mechanism of action.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: A **polyfunctional** compound has identical functional groups (glycerol — 3 OH), a **heterofunctional** compound has different groups (lactic acid — OH and COOH; amino acids — NH~2~ and COOH). Most metabolites are heterofunctional.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The series of dicarboxylic acids (C~2~–C~5~): **“Oh My, Such Good”** — oxalic, malonic, succinic, glutaric.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Ethylene glycol** (antifreeze) tastes sweet but is highly toxic: in the body it is oxidized to glycolaldehyde, glyoxylic and **oxalic** acid — severe acidosis and kidney damage by calcium oxalate crystals result. The antidote is fomepizole or ethanol.

blocks.text: Alcohols are mono-, di- or polyhydric by the number of hydroxyl groups, and primary, secondary or tertiary by the carbon that bears the OH. In **aromatic alcohols** the OH is attached not to the benzene ring but to a side chain (benzyl alcohol C~6~H~5~CH~2~OH); compounds with OH attached directly to the ring are called **phenols**.

items: **Ethanol** — its 70 % solution denatures proteins and has the strongest antiseptic action (96 % alcohol coagulates protein on the surface of microbes so quickly that it does not penetrate inside).
**Benzyl alcohol** — a preservative in injection solutions; toxic in newborns (“gasping syndrome”).
**Menthol** (a cyclic alcohol) — a cooling and distracting effect (validol, ointments).

blocks.title: Table 10.1. Polyhydric alcohols
head: Substance
Formula
Significance
rows: part of lipids (triglycerides, phospholipids); base for ointments and suppositories, laxative
sugar substitute; accumulates in the lens and nerves and contributes to diabetic complications

blocks.text: **Qualitative reaction:** in an alkaline medium polyhydric alcohols dissolve the Cu(OH)~2~ precipitate and form a **deep blue** complex (copper glycerate) — monohydric alcohols do not give this reaction. This is due to the increased acidity of neighboring OH groups and the formation of a chelate.

**Polyhydric phenols:** pyrocatechol (1,2-dihydroxybenzene), resorcinol (1,3-), hydroquinone (1,4-). The pyrocatechol residue is part of the **catecholamines**. Hydroquinone is easily oxidized to **quinone** and reduced back again: this reversible system is the basis of the work of **ubiquinone (coenzyme Q)** in the respiratory chain.

parts.text: In diabetes mellitus, during hyperglycemia glucose is reduced to sorbitol by **aldose reductase**. Sorbitol crosses membranes poorly and accumulates in the cells of the lens, nerves and kidneys, causing osmotic swelling — one mechanism of the development of **cataract, neuropathy and nephropathy**.

blocks.text: **Polyamines** are compounds with two or more amino groups. They are formed by decarboxylation of amino acids: **putrescine** H~2~N(CH~2~)~4~NH~2~ from ornithine and **cadaverine** H~2~N(CH~2~)~5~NH~2~ from lysine; **spermidine** and **spermine** are synthesized from putrescine.

items: At physiological pH polyamines carry several positive charges and bind to negatively charged **DNA and RNA**, stabilizing their structure; they are needed for cell division and growth.
Polyamines increase in rapidly dividing tissues and in **tumors**; inhibitors of the enzyme of their synthesis (ornithine decarboxylase), such as eflornithine, are used in treatment.
Putrescine and cadaverine are foul-smelling “cadaveric poisons” (ptomaines) formed when proteins putrefy.

Formula
Biological and medical significance
rows: calcium oxalate stones; a product of ethylene glycol poisoning
a **competitive inhibitor** of succinate dehydrogenase; malonyl-CoA — in fatty acid synthesis
a Krebs cycle metabolite; FAD-dependent dehydrogenation turns it into fumarate
a metabolite of the Krebs and urea cycles

blocks.text: **The succinate dehydrogenase reaction:** HOOC−CH~2~−CH~2~−COOH + FAD → HOOC−CH=CH−COOH + FADH~2~. Because malonate resembles succinate in structure, it binds to the active site of the enzyme but is not dehydrogenated — the classic example of **competitive inhibition**.

items: **Ethanolamine (colamine)** HO−CH~2~−CH~2~−NH~2~ — part of the phospholipid phosphatidylethanolamine (cephalin); formed by decarboxylation of serine.
**Choline** HO−CH~2~−CH~2~−N^+^(CH~3~)~3~ — part of phosphatidylcholine (lecithin); protects the liver from fatty degeneration (a lipotropic factor).
**Acetylcholine** CH~3~CO−O−CH~2~CH~2~−N^+^(CH~3~)~3~ — the ester of choline, the mediator of parasympathetic and neuromuscular synapses; it is rapidly broken down by acetylcholinesterase.

blocks.text: **Catecholamines** are biogenic amines containing a pyrocatechol ring and an aminoethyl chain: **dopamine**, **norepinephrine** (noradrenaline) and **epinephrine** (adrenaline). They are synthesized from tyrosine: tyrosine → DOPA → dopamine → norepinephrine → epinephrine.

blocks.label: Figure 10.1
blocks.caption: Catecholamines: dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine — amino alcohols containing a pyrocatechol ring, a β-hydroxyl and an amino group (structural formulas drawn with RDKit).

parts.text: Organophosphate insecticides (chlorophos, malathion) and nerve agents irreversibly phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates: miosis, salivation, bronchospasm, convulsions. Treatment is **atropine** (an M-cholinergic blocker) and **oximes** that reactivate the enzyme. **Epinephrine** is the drug of first choice in anaphylactic shock.

product of anaerobic glycolysis (lactate); Krebs cycle; a ketone body; citrate — an anticoagulant (blood preservation)

blocks.text: Important reactions of heterofunctional acids: **lactate ⇄ pyruvate** (lactate dehydrogenase, NAD^+^/NADH); **pyruvate → acetyl-CoA + CO~2~** (oxidative decarboxylation); **decarboxylation of β-keto acids**: acetoacetate → acetone + CO~2~ (the smell of acetone on the breath in diabetes); **transamination**: amino acid + keto acid ⇄ new keto acid + new amino acid.

parts.text: Citrate binds Ca^2+^ ions (a chelate) and stops blood clotting — **sodium citrate** is used as an anticoagulant in stored blood and laboratory tubes. When blood with much citrate is transfused rapidly, hypocalcemia may develop — calcium preparations are given.

parts.text: **Paracetamol poisoning:** in a large dose part of the drug is converted in the liver into the toxic metabolite **NAPQI**; once glutathione (a thiol) is used up, NAPQI damages the proteins of hepatocytes. The antidote is **N-acetylcysteine**, which restores the glutathione supply. This clearly shows the protective role of the thiol group.

skills.title: Skill: detecting polyhydric alcohols (the Cu(OH)~2~ reaction)

items: Put 2 drops of CuSO~4~ and 1 mL of 10 % NaOH into a test tube — a light blue precipitate of Cu(OH)~2~ forms.
Prepare two tubes: add glycerol to one and ethanol to the other.
Shake and observe: in the tube with glycerol the precipitate dissolves and a deep blue solution forms.
In the tube with ethanol there is no change (a monohydric alcohol).
Conclusion: neighboring OH groups form a chelate complex of copper.

skills.title: Skill: functional analysis of a compound

items: Mark all functional groups in the formula (−OH, −NH~2~, −COOH, C=O, −SH).
If the groups are identical — a polyfunctional compound; if different — heterofunctional.
Determine the relative position of the groups (α, β, γ or ortho, meta, para).
List the reactions each group gives (salt, ester, amide, oxidation).
Link the significance of the substance as a metabolite or drug with this structure.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A car-repair shop worker drank antifreeze by mistake. A few hours later he appeared drunk, and then metabolic acidosis (pH 7.15) developed; many crystals were found in the urine, and urine output decreased.
cases.ask: Explain the chemical basis of the poisoning. What crystals were found in the urine, and what is the treatment?
cases.answer: The **ethylene glycol** in antifreeze is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase to glycolaldehyde → glycolic acid → glyoxylic acid → **oxalic acid**. The acids cause acidosis; oxalate forms poorly soluble **calcium oxalate** crystals with Ca^2+^ and damages the renal tubules (acute kidney injury). Treatment: **fomepizole** or ethanol (they occupy alcohol dehydrogenase competitively), sodium bicarbonate, hemodialysis.

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: After working with an organophosphate insecticide, a gardener was brought in with constricted pupils, heavy salivation and sweating, shortness of breath and muscle twitching.
cases.ask: What is the biochemical cause of the symptoms? Which drugs are given?
cases.answer: The organophosphate irreversibly phosphorylates the serine in the active site of **acetylcholinesterase**. Acetylcholine is not broken down and accumulates in the synapses, constantly stimulating muscarinic (miosis, salivation, bronchospasm) and nicotinic (muscle twitching, then paralysis) receptors. Treatment: **atropine** (blocks M-cholinergic receptors) in large doses, **oximes** that reactivate the enzyme (pralidoxime), respiratory support.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A patient took 15 g of paracetamol within 1 day for a headache. At first there are no symptoms except nausea.
cases.ask: What is the danger? Explain the chemical mechanism and the action of the antidote.
cases.answer: The danger is severe liver damage (fulminant hepatitis). At normal doses paracetamol is conjugated with glucuronic and sulfuric acids and excreted; at large doses these pathways become saturated and much toxic **NAPQI** is formed via cytochrome P450. NAPQI is normally neutralized by the SH group of **glutathione**; once glutathione is used up, it binds to hepatocyte proteins and causes necrosis (symptoms appear after 1–3 days). **N-acetylcysteine**, as a source of cysteine, restores glutathione synthesis; the earlier it is given, the more effective it is.
